subject: AI & Agents
title: AlphaGo: The Game Nobody Thought AI Could Win
description: A fast breakdown of AlphaGo: The Game Nobody Thought AI Could Win for builders.

hook.text: Go has more possible positions than atoms in the universe. In 2016, AI mastered it.

buildup.text: DeepMind's AlphaGo combined deep learning with Monte Carlo tree search.

discovery.text: It beat world champion Lee Sedol 4-1. Move 37 in Game 2 was unlike anything a human had ever played.

twist.text: Lee Sedol's single winning game — his 'divine move' — brought the audience to tears.

climax.text: AlphaGo Zero later surpassed it by learning entirely from self-play — no human games needed.

punchline.text: The machine didn't just beat humans. It invented new moves.

quiz.question: What made AlphaGo's Move 37 remarkable?
options: It was a strategy no human had ever played
It was the fastest move ever made
It was identical to a famous historical game

details.summary: DeepMind's AlphaGo defeated Go world champion Lee Sedol in 2016, conquering a game with more positions than atoms in the universe. It had been widely believed that Go would resist AI for decades more.
details.whyItMatters: AlphaGo shattered assumptions about AI's limits and demonstrated that deep learning combined with search could solve problems once considered intractable. It accelerated AI ambition globally.
takeaways: AlphaGo defeated world Go champion Lee Sedol 4 to 1 in 2016
Go has more possible positions than atoms in the observable universe
The victory came decades earlier than experts predicted

faq.question: Why was Go considered harder for AI than chess?
faq.answer: Go has roughly 10^170 possible positions compared to chess's 10^47. Brute-force search is impossible. Winning requires intuition and pattern recognition that seemed uniquely human until AlphaGo proved otherwise.

faq.question: How did AlphaGo learn to play Go?
faq.answer: It combined deep neural networks with Monte Carlo tree search. It first learned from human expert games, then improved through millions of games of self-play, eventually surpassing all human players.
